blocks.content: Picture a mid size company. Two thousand employees. Each one needs access to Slack, Salesforce, an HR tool, an analytics dashboard, a design tool, and a dozen other SaaS apps.
Now multiply that by two thousand people and you get a real mess. Thousands of separate passwords sitting in thousands of browsers, notebooks, and probably a few sticky notes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396366502-80973780.png
blocks.alt: Employee juggling separate logins for four different SaaS tools

blocks.content: IT hates this. Every new hire needs an account created in a dozen different tools. Every employee who leaves needs their access revoked in all of those same tools, and if IT forgets even one, that ex employee still has a working login into company data.
SAML exists to solve exactly this problem. One login at a trusted central place, and every other tool just trusts that login instead of asking for its own password.
This is the enterprise single sign on story, and SAML is one of the oldest and still most widely used protocols that makes it work.
1. Introduction

SAML stands for Security Assertion Markup Language. It is an XML based standard for exchanging authentication information between two parties, so that a user can log in once and be trusted everywhere.
It was built for exactly the enterprise problem above: one company, many internal SaaS tools, one workforce that needs to move between them without re typing a password every single time.
1.1 The password sprawl problem
Without SAML, every SaaS tool your company uses manages its own list of usernames and passwords. That sounds fine at first, until you look at what it actually costs.

["Weak passwords everywhere employees reuse the same password across a dozen tools because remembering twelve unique ones is unrealistic.","Slow onboarding a new hire needs a manually created account in every single tool before they can do any work.","Incomplete offboarding when someone leaves, IT has to remember to disable their account in every tool separately. Miss one and that access stays alive.","No central visibility security teams cannot easily answer a simple question like who currently has access to our finance tool."]
items: Weak passwords everywhere employees reuse the same password across a dozen tools because remembering twelve unique ones is unrealistic.
Slow onboarding a new hire needs a manually created account in every single tool before they can do any work.
Incomplete offboarding when someone leaves, IT has to remember to disable their account in every tool separately. Miss one and that access stays alive.
No central visibility security teams cannot easily answer a simple question like who currently has access to our finance tool.

blocks.title: The real cost
blocks.content: The offboarding problem is the scary one. A disgruntled ex employee with a forgotten login into a customer database is a real, recurring security incident, not a hypothetical.
1.2 What SAML actually gives you
SAML lets a company centralize identity in one place, and lets every other tool simply trust that central place instead of keeping its own password database.
An employee logs into one central portal once. From there, they can open any connected SaaS tool and land inside already authenticated, no separate password required.
Turn off that one central account and every connected tool becomes unreachable for that person immediately. Offboarding becomes a single click instead of a checklist across twelve admin panels.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396366502-333016539.png
blocks.alt: Identity Provider centrally managing multiple employee identities

blocks.content: 2. The core actors
Every SAML conversation involves exactly two parties talking about a user. Understanding these two roles is really the whole mental model.
2.1 The Identity Provider, IdP

The Identity Provider is where the company centrally manages who its employees are and checks their passwords. Okta, Azure AD, also known as Microsoft Entra ID, OneLogin, and Google Workspace are common real world IdPs.
This is the one place that actually knows the employee real password. It authenticates the person, and once satisfied, it is willing to vouch for them to any other trusted application.
2.2 The Service Provider, SP
The Service Provider is the actual SaaS application the employee wants to use: the analytics dashboard, the CRM, the HR portal, whatever the tool is.
The SP does not want to be in the business of storing passwords either. Instead it delegates the whole login step to a trusted IdP and just asks, did this person already prove who they are.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396366503-487271457.png
blocks.alt: Employee requesting access to a Service Provider application

blocks.content: 2.3 The trust relationship between them

This whole system only works because the SP and the IdP have agreed, ahead of time, to trust each other. That agreement is configured once by an admin on both sides, usually by exchanging metadata and a signing certificate.
Once that trust is set up, the SP knows exactly whose signature to check on any assertion it receives, and will reject anything signed by someone else.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396366503-628647987.png
blocks.alt: Trust relationship configured once between the Identity Provider and the Service Provider

blocks.title: This is a one time setup step
blocks.content: An admin configures this trust relationship once, typically by uploading the IdP metadata file or certificate into the SP admin settings. After that, it just works for every employee.
3. How the SAML flow works
At a conceptual level, the whole flow is a small dance between the employee browser, the SP, and the IdP. No passwords ever pass through the SP.
3.1 Step by step

["Step 1 The employee tries to open the SP, for example an analytics dashboard.","Step 2 The SP notices there is no active session for this employee and redirects their browser to the IdP.","Step 3 If the employee is not already logged into the IdP, they authenticate there, usually with a password plus multi factor authentication.","Step 4 The IdP builds a signed XML assertion, essentially a statement saying this is definitely this specific employee, verified just now.","Step 5 The browser carries that assertion back to the SP.","Step 6 The SP checks the signature, confirms the assertion is genuine and unexpired, and logs the employee in."]
items: Step 1 The employee tries to open the SP, for example an analytics dashboard.
Step 2 The SP notices there is no active session for this employee and redirects their browser to the IdP.
Step 3 If the employee is not already logged into the IdP, they authenticate there, usually with a password plus multi factor authentication.
Step 4 The IdP builds a signed XML assertion, essentially a statement saying this is definitely this specific employee, verified just now.
Step 5 The browser carries that assertion back to the SP.
Step 6 The SP checks the signature, confirms the assertion is genuine and unexpired, and logs the employee in.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396366503-626453577.png
blocks.alt: Service Provider redirecting the employee browser to the Identity Provider to log in

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396366504-614077880.png
blocks.alt: Identity Provider generating a signed assertion and sending it to the Service Provider

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396366504-387000247.png
blocks.alt: Service Provider verifying the assertion signature before trusting the login

blocks.content: Notice what never happens here. The employee real password is typed once, into the IdP, and the SP never sees it at all. The SP only ever sees a signed assertion.
3.2 Why the assertion has to be signed
blocks.text: 3.2 Why the assertion has to be signed

blocks.content: Anyone can craft an XML document that claims to be about a particular employee. The signature is what turns that claim into something the SP can actually trust.

The IdP signs the assertion using its private key. The SP, which already has the IdP public certificate from the trust setup step, verifies that signature matches. If it does not match, or the assertion has been altered even slightly after signing, verification fails and the login is rejected.
The signature answers one question: did this assertion genuinely come from our trusted IdP, unmodified. Without it, anyone could forge a login.

blocks.title: Common real world bug
blocks.content: A classic SAML vulnerability class is XML signature wrapping, where an attacker adds a forged assertion alongside a legitimately signed one and tricks a poorly written verifier into checking the signature on one node but reading identity data from another. This is exactly why teams use well tested SAML libraries instead of writing XML parsing by hand.
4. SP initiated versus IdP initiated flows
blocks.text: 4. SP initiated versus IdP initiated flows

blocks.content: There are two ways this login dance can actually start, depending on where the employee begins.
4.1 SP initiated flow

The employee starts by directly opening the app they want, say by typing the analytics tool URL into their browser. The SP notices they are not logged in yet and kicks off the redirect to the IdP itself.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396368395-694163002.png
blocks.alt: SP initiated flow starting from the application and redirecting to the Identity Provider

blocks.content: This is the more common everyday case. You just go straight to the tool you want to use, and SAML quietly handles the rest behind the scenes.
4.2 IdP initiated flow
The employee starts at a company SSO portal or dashboard, something like a tile based launcher inside Okta, and clicks on the analytics tool tile directly from there.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396368397-712779688.png
blocks.alt: IdP initiated flow starting from the company SSO portal and going straight to the chosen app

blocks.content: In this case the IdP already knows the employee is authenticated, since they are sitting inside its portal, so it builds the assertion immediately and sends the browser straight to the SP with it.

blocks.title: A subtle security gotcha
blocks.content: IdP initiated flows are slightly more exposed to replay style attacks because there is no fresh request from the SP to correlate against. Most modern IdPs mitigate this with short assertion validity windows and one time use tracking.
5. What a SAML assertion actually looks like
blocks.text: 5. What a SAML assertion actually looks like

blocks.content: All of this trust me, this is the user talk eventually boils down to an actual XML document flowing over the network. Let us look at a simplified one.
5.1 A simplified assertion
Real assertions from Okta or Azure AD carry more attributes and namespaces, but this stripped down version shows the pieces that matter.

<saml:Assertion ID="_a1b2c3" IssueInstant="2026-07-09T10:15:00Z">
  <saml:Issuer>https://company.okta.com</saml:Issuer>

  <ds:Signature>
    <!-- signed digest of this whole assertion, using the IdP private key -->
  </ds:Signature>

  <saml:Subject>
    <saml:NameID>priya.sharma@company.com</saml:NameID>
  </saml:Subject>

  <saml:Conditions NotBefore="2026-07-09T10:15:00Z" NotOnOrAfter="2026-07-09T10:20:00Z" />

  <saml:AttributeStatement>
    <saml:Attribute Name="email">
      <saml:AttributeValue>priya.sharma@company.com</saml:AttributeValue>
    </saml:Attribute>
    <saml:Attribute Name="role">
      <saml:AttributeValue>analyst</saml:AttributeValue>
    </saml:Attribute>
  </saml:AttributeStatement>
</saml:Assertion>

blocks.content: 5.2 Verifying the signature in code

On the SP side, verifying an incoming assertion is not something you should hand write. In practice you lean on a battle tested library, for example xml-crypto or a full SAML SDK like passport-saml in Node.js.
Notice the shape of the logic. Parse the XML, find the signature block, check it against the known IdP public certificate, and only trust the subject and attributes if that check passes.

blocks.title: Do not skip the expiry check
blocks.content: A signature can be perfectly valid on an assertion that is ten hours old. Always check the Conditions window too, otherwise a captured old assertion could be replayed by an attacker.
6. SAML versus OAuth and OIDC
If you have worked with login flows before, you have probably run into OAuth or OpenID Connect, OIDC. It is worth briefly placing SAML next to them, without turning this into a full OAuth tutorial.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396368397-27927041.png
blocks.alt: SAML XML based enterprise SSO compared against OAuth OIDC JSON based consumer and API use

blocks.content: {"headers":["SAML","OAuth / OIDC"],"rows":[["Older standard, mid 2000s era","Newer standard, mostly 2010s onward"],["XML based assertions","JSON based tokens, usually JWT"],["Historically enterprise and SSO focused","Common for consumer apps and public APIs"],["Identity Provider and Service Provider","Authorization server and client, plus resource server"],["Great fit for company internal SSO portals","Great fit for letting a mobile app or website login with Google, and for API access delegation"]]}

Plenty of modern enterprise tools support both, and let the customer IT admin choose whichever their existing identity setup already speaks. Neither one is strictly better, they solve overlapping but not identical problems.
7. Worked example, logging into an analytics tool
blocks.text: 7. Worked example, logging into an analytics tool

blocks.content: Let us walk through a concrete case: an employee named Priya at a company that uses Okta as its IdP, trying to open a third party analytics SaaS tool.
7.1 What actually happens

blocks.title: Priya opens the analytics dashboard
blocks.text: Priya types analytics.example.com into her browser. The analytics tool, acting as the SP, checks for an active session and finds none.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396368398-997442520.png
blocks.alt: Employee logging into an analytics tool via Okta issuing a signed assertion

blocks.content: ["The analytics tool redirects Priya browser to https://company.okta.com with a SAML authentication request.","Priya is already logged into Okta from earlier that morning, so no password prompt appears again, Okta recognizes her session instantly.","Okta generates a signed assertion identifying her as priya.sharma@company.com, with her role attribute set to analyst.","Her browser posts that signed assertion to the analytics tool login endpoint.","The analytics tool verifies the signature against Okta known public certificate, confirms it is fresh and intact, and logs Priya straight into her dashboard."]
items: The analytics tool redirects Priya browser to https://company.okta.com with a SAML authentication request.
Priya is already logged into Okta from earlier that morning, so no password prompt appears again, Okta recognizes her session instantly.
Okta generates a signed assertion identifying her as priya.sharma@company.com, with her role attribute set to analyst.
Her browser posts that signed assertion to the analytics tool login endpoint.
The analytics tool verifies the signature against Okta known public certificate, confirms it is fresh and intact, and logs Priya straight into her dashboard.

blocks.content: From Priya point of view this whole thing felt instant. She typed a URL and landed on her dashboard. No separate password, no separate account creation, nothing to remember.
7.2 What happens when Priya leaves the company
blocks.text: 7.2 What happens when Priya leaves the company

blocks.content: This is really where the design pays off. When Priya offboards, IT disables exactly one account, her Okta identity.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396368398-937307130.png
blocks.alt: Disabling one Identity Provider account removing access to every connected app at once

blocks.content: The moment that happens, every SAML connected tool she used, the analytics dashboard, the CRM, the HR portal, all of it, becomes unreachable for her. There is no separate checklist of a dozen admin panels to visit.
8. Real world usage
SAML is not an academic protocol, it runs quietly behind a huge amount of everyday enterprise software.

["Okta one of the most widely used IdPs, especially at mid size and growing companies.","Azure AD, now Microsoft Entra ID extremely common at companies already deep in the Microsoft ecosystem.","OneLogin another established enterprise IdP with the same core role.","Google Workspace can also act as an IdP for smaller companies already using Gmail and Google Docs internally."]
items: Okta one of the most widely used IdPs, especially at mid size and growing companies.
Azure AD, now Microsoft Entra ID extremely common at companies already deep in the Microsoft ecosystem.
OneLogin another established enterprise IdP with the same core role.
Google Workspace can also act as an IdP for smaller companies already using Gmail and Google Docs internally.

blocks.content: On the other side, nearly every serious B2B SaaS product, from project management tools to analytics platforms to CRMs, lists SAML SSO as a feature, almost always gated behind their enterprise pricing tier.
9. The interview angle

If a system design interview mentions the product targets enterprise customers, SSO support is one of those requirements that experienced interviewers expect you to bring up yourself, without being prompted.
Enterprise buyers genuinely ask about SAML SSO support during procurement. It is not a nice to have, it is frequently a hard requirement before a deal closes.

["Mentioning SAML shows you understand a real non functional requirement that pure feature focused designs tend to miss.","You do not need to draw the full XML flow on a whiteboard, just show you know the IdP and SP roles, and why the SP never sees the actual password.","A good follow up point: SAML is usually additive, most products also support username and password login alongside SAML SSO for smaller customers who have no IdP at all."]
items: Mentioning SAML shows you understand a real non functional requirement that pure feature focused designs tend to miss.
You do not need to draw the full XML flow on a whiteboard, just show you know the IdP and SP roles, and why the SP never sees the actual password.
A good follow up point: SAML is usually additive, most products also support username and password login alongside SAML SSO for smaller customers who have no IdP at all.

The one sentence version: SAML lets a company vouch for its employees once, centrally, and signed, so every connected SaaS tool can trust that vouching instead of managing its own separate password for every single person.
